column1: The pro-choice editors of the journal California Medicine made this very point in 1970

column1: It has been necessary to separate the idea of abortion from the idea of killing
column2: which continues to be socially abhorrent. The result has been a curious avoidance of the scientific fact
column3: which everyone really knows

column1: Regret Denial at the March For Life

column2: or protest (methinks too much) that abortion regret is very “rare.”

column1: I observed both sides in action at the recent March for Life. There had to be at least 150
column2: 000 marchers this year. It was a massive turnout. Among them were many women who carried signs saying “I regret my abortion
column3: ” as part of the Silent No More campaign.

column1: Prior to the March for Life
column2: some of the regretters––along with many pro-life demonstrators––were in front of the Supreme Court building
column3: the endpoint of the march. There were also about two dozen pro-choice counter-protesters gathered there at the time. (They dispersed with the massive arrival of the marchers an hour or so later.) I watched as one regretter gave personal
column4: heartfelt testimony. Then the counter-protesters went into full denial mode.

column1: They tried to drown her out with loud chants of “Facts not given!” Of course

column3: ” the first of the five stages of grief is denial. The emotionally stable person arrives at the final stage––acceptance––after going through mid-stages Kubler-Ross identified as anger
column4: bargaining (rationalizing)

column1: But by coming to terms with the reality
column2: abortion regretters go through the stages of grieving. The anger stage is probably magnified for many who felt coerced into their abortion by boyfriends

column3: and bitter group of people. As one abortion regretter told me on the spot

column7: anxiety

column1: Abortion is such a profound event in one’s life

column1: Student debt increased by a whopping 107 percent between 2009 and 2019. Americans now owe $1.6 trillion in education loans. Policy wonks and politicians respond by concocting flashy plans that hardly solve the debt crisis.

Debt forgiveness plans like Sens. Elizabeth Warren’s and Bernie Sanders’s will encourage colleges to increase their already pricey tuitions. Proposals to restructure repayment programs or dip into retirement accounts don’t prevent students from taking out dangerous amounts of student loans in the first place. We need to help students before they’re drowning in debt.

column2: teachers

column2: the return on investment for higher education has steadily declined. More than 40 percent of recent college graduates are underemployed and work in jobs that do not require a college education. Underemployed graduates get stuck in such positions
column3: drastically shrinking their lifetime earnings.

column1: Given these bleak prospects

column1: Student debt increased by a whopping 107 percent between 2009 and 2019. Americans now owe $1.6 trillion in education loans. Policy wonks and politicians respond by concocting flashy plans that hardly solve the debt crisis.

Debt forgiveness plans like Sens. Elizabeth Warren’s and Bernie Sanders’s will encourage colleges to increase their already pricey tuitions. Proposals to restructure repayment programs or dip into retirement accounts don’t prevent students from taking out dangerous amounts of student loans in the first place. column2: teachers
column3: and other leaders need to encourage alternative options for these students. These students are the least likely to get well-paid jobs that will allow them to repay their college loans. This will leave them in a terrible financial trap.

column2: the return on investment for higher education has steadily declined. More than 40 percent of recent college graduates are underemployed and work in jobs that do not require a college education. Underemployed graduates get stuck in such positions
column3: drastically shrinking their lifetime earnings.

column2: teachers

column5: they should earn money while they “find themselves

Climate initiatives also get stuck because the momentum they generate is not always in the direction of substantial change or decarbonization. For instance
column2: moving from coal-fired to natural gas electricity production can lower emissions. However
column3: turning to this bridge fuel reinforces dependence on fossil energy. Political coalitions that support and benefit from such an initial change might not favour more aggressive action.

column1: A case in point is Colorado’s New Energy Economy policy. In the mid-2000s

column3: however

column1: These dynamics apply equally to individuals. Studies show that nudging people to change their daily practices can decrease their support for broader
column2: transformative policies because they feel they have done enough.

column1: Getting unstuck

Our research has identified four questions to ask when designing and implementing climate action to counter these dynamics: Does it disrupt dependence on fossil energy? Does it build coalitions that favour more aggressive actions? Is it sensitive to broader connections? Does it spark climate action elsewhere?

These questions suggest a need to value the transformative potential of any climate action rather than (only) the immediate emissions reductions. Quick emissions reductions like those generated by fuel switching are seductive but can stall. Instead policy-makers should evaluate climate action on whether it contributes to disrupting reliance on fossil energy and reinforcing alternative paths.
Getting unstuck also requires thinking beyond single policies. A successful EV policy like Norway’s pays attention to the entire personal transport sector (taxes and subsidies
column2: infrastructure
column3: etc.). It has even catalyzed change in the broader transportation sector
column4: including electric ferries and aviation.

column1: Moreover
column2: the politics of getting started are different than the politics of maintaining and extending climate action. One way to create broader coalitions of support is to build justice and equity into every climate action. Overly technocratic climate initiatives
column3: such as smart cities
column4: can get stuck and fail to catalyze broad decarbonization in part because they fail to generate broad and diverse coalitions to build on initial successes.

column1: Building a better society is not possible without addressing climate change. Addressing climate change is not politically feasible without pursuing a more just and equitable society to ensure broad support.

column1: Student debt increased by a whopping 107 percent between 2009 and 2019. Americans now owe $1.6 trillion in education loans. Policy wonks and politicians respond by concocting flashy plans that hardly solve the debt crisis.

Debt forgiveness plans like Sens. Elizabeth Warren’s and Bernie Sanders’s will encourage colleges to increase their already pricey tuitions. Proposals to restructure repayment programs or dip into retirement accounts don’t prevent students from taking out dangerous amounts of student loans in the first place. We need to help students before they’re drowning in debt.

column2: teachers
column3: and other leaders need to encourage alternative options for these students. These students are the least likely to get well-paid jobs that will allow them to repay their college loans. This will leave them in a terrible financial trap.

column1: It’s a trap because a college education doesn’t guarantee a good job. For years
column2: the return on investment for higher education has steadily declined. More than 40 percent of recent college graduates are underemployed and work in jobs that do not require a college education. Underemployed graduates get stuck in such positions
column3: drastically shrinking their lifetime earnings.

column1: Given these bleak prospects
column2: students who go to college to “find themselves” are likely to waste precious time and money because they lack a clear vision. Thirty-three percent of students change majors and 10 percent switch majors multiple times
column3: which prolongs the completion time and cost of a bachelor’s degree.

column1: College also exacts a high cost from students who lack sufficient academic preparation. column2: teachers
column3: and other leaders should carefully note these trends and consider tailoring their career advice to each student’s specific needs. Most American policymakers say all students should attend college

column3: volunteer positions

column5: they should earn money while they “find themselves

column3: Republicans control the Senate

column1: The Democratic candidates missed the opportunity last week in Nevada—a state with a 30 percent Latino population—to address the root causes of our immigration crisis. They predictably criticized the worst Trump administration immigration policies

column4: but we cannot ignore that many people come to the United States in the first place because our foreign policies—by both Democrats and Republicans—force them to leave their homes in Latin America and elsewhere.

column1: The U.S. displaces its neighbors by displacing their governments. column2: however. She used this weekend’s news cycle to continue highlighting the evils of wealth inequality

column1: On Monday

column3: such as Bill Gates
column4: may well be good people. But “a system that allows billionaires to exist when there are parts of Alabama where people are still getting ringworm because they don’t have access to public health is wrong.”

column1: AOC continued to hammer this point home later the same night on “The Late Show” with Stephen Colbert
column2: explaining (yet again) that her proposed 70 percent marginal income tax rate would only be on money made above the first $10 million a year — and that a similar marginal tax rate reached 90% when Dwight Eisenhower was president.

column1: “Do we want to live in a city where billionaires have their own personal Uber helipads
column2: ” she asked
column3: “in the same city and same society as people who are working 80-hour weeks and can’t feed their kids?”

column1: Right-wing media sprung into action to try to discredit her
column2: of course
column3: by implying that a woman who graduated summa cum laude with an economics degree is a bimbo and with Twitchy using a screenshot to make the usually genial Ocasio-Cortez somehow look like a ballbuster. But it’s getting increasingly difficult to maintain the myth that the enormous wealth inequality in not just American society but the entire world somehow reflect a system that’s fairly rewarding people for their talent and labor.

column1: On his own
column2: the barely literate imbecile with no redeeming qualities who sits in the Oval Office claiming to be a billionaire (even if he probably isn’t) creates a one-man argument against the premise that wealth flows from merit. But the numbers increasingly back up Ocasio-Cortez’s argument that our system unjustly concentrating massive amounts of wealth in the hands of a few
column3: leaving the rest of society with little to show for all their hard work and social contributions.

column1: On Monday
column2: Oxfam published a report showing that a mere 26 individual billionaires now have as much wealth between them as the least wealthy half of the human population. Which is to say
column3: these 26 people have more money combined than 3.8 billion of the world’s population.

column1: The idea that those 26 people are somehow being fairly rewarded by that massively unequal equation defies all common sense
column2: especially as most billionaires have built their wealth on the labor of people who only take home a fraction of the value they add to the companies they work for.

column1: It’s not just a matter of sour grapes. The billionaires saw their wealth rise by 12 percent in one year — the same year that saw the poorest half of the population lose 11 percent of their wealth
column2: a loss that people who are already struggling to afford food
column3: shelter and basic necessities simply cannot tolerate.

column1: It’s not just that there seems to be a direct correlation between how much money the rich make and how little everyone else gets. There’s also evidence that vast inequalities stifle economic growth
column2: and that redistribution of the sort that Ocasio-Cortez proposes can kickstart the economy. Money in the hands of working people is spent
column3: and stimulates the economy
column4: much more than money being hoarded by the wealthy few
column5: after all. Inequality also breeds crime and other forms of social instability.

column1: But mostly
column2: this is a moral issue
column3: and one of Ocasio-Cortez’s remarkable gifts as a communicator is her ability to speak about this issue in moral terms. Most people
column4: of all wealth and income levels are hard workers. The fact that only a select few are amply rewarded while most others go wanting is both unfair and immoral. And the worse the problem gets
column5: the more unavoidable this unfairness becomes.

column1: Nearly 60 percent of Americans now support the marginal tax rate program Ocasio-Cortez has proposed. This includes a remarkable 45 percent of Republicans
column2: despite all the work right-wing media has done to demonize Ocasio-Cortez and anything related to her.

column1: The problem conservatives must face is that the very inequality they are defending is a rhetorical obstacle in itself. Most people recognize that it’s unfair that rich people make so much more money than the rest of us
column2: and does not necessarily prove they have worked harder. Getting people to sign off on the idea that they simply are less worthy than their wealthier fellow citizens is not an easy lift
column3: which is why Republicans prefer to stick to culture-war distractions
column4: like fear-mongering over immigration or abortion.

column1: Since Ocasio-Cortez first mentioned the 70 percent tax rate on CNN
column2: a number of mansplaining journalists have written harrumphing pieces explaining that the “real” problem is tax loopholes or capital-gains tax rates set too low. This approach fails to understand the nature and purpose of Ocasio-Cortez’s political rhetoric. Any tax plan that raised marginal rates that high would almost certainly have other provisions to close loopholes or tax investments more fairly. But before we can get to that point
column3: there must be more political momentum to change the tax system.

column1: By focusing on marginal tax rates — which are easier to explain to the general public than most other taxation strategies — Ocasio-Cortez can help build a moral and social argument against economic inequality. Blunt statements
column2: like saying that it’s immoral that billionaires exist at all
column3: can help people reimagine a world where resources are distributed more equitably and ordinary people who work hard and drive economic growth can see their effort reflected in their paychecks.

column1: Because the truth of the matter is that she’s right: We shouldn’t have billionaires. Any system that has a handful of ultra-wealthy individuals
column2: by definition
column3: is not rewarding hard work and social contributions fairly
column4: or anywhere close to it. We don’t need to embrace full-on socialism communism
column5: and Ocasio-Cortez is swift to say that. But the floor needs to come up and the ceiling needs to come down. Most people know that’s true
column6: whatever their official “politics” may be
column7: and it’s becoming increasingly difficult to deny it.";['evils'

column1: Unlike many writers sympathetic to nationalism and populism

column1: ‘Negative Piety’

column2: author of The Open Society and Its Enemies
column3: as a preeminent apostle of this “negative piety.” Popper argued that the Western philosophical tradition inaugurated by Plato was oppressive because it sought to know the truth
column4: and “insofar as truth is known
column5: it must be affirmed

column3: openness
column4: and weakness to dissolve the “strong beliefs and powerful loyalties thought to have fueled the conflicts that convulsed the twentieth century.” For instance
column5: the project of the European Union is not just of easier trade and travel

column1: Reno demonstrates the development and eventual dominance of this viewpoint by examining a variety of figures
column2: including George H. W. Bush
column3: Friedrich Hayek
column4: Albert Camus

column1: Reno does overlook John Lennon

column1: Becoming Homeless

Advocates of the postwar consensus point to populist outbreaks as evidence that these repressive measures are necessary to protect the open society from its enemies. But the current populisms in the West are responses to the excess and failures of the postwar consensus
column2: not to its absence. The immediate danger is not that of dark
column3: strong gods
column4: but of a vacuum. Our problems are not those of a closed society
column5: but of one that is too open. We are not suffering from too much solidarity and loyalty
column6: but dissolution.

column1: This is exemplified by a leadership class that is disloyal to those it seeks to lead. On issues of economics and immigration
column2: the rhetoric of openness has gone hand in hand with the ruthless exploitation of cheap labor and the disavowal of economic solidarity with fellow citizens. As Reno notes
column3: “Our center-left leadership class will promise to subsidize working-class consumption
column4: but it won’t reorient the global economy toward their employment.” Welfare
column5: yes; jobs
column6: no—just give the proles some cash so they can distract themselves with cheap consumer goods made in China. The costs of working-class decline are just one more thing for corporations to outsource.

column1: Populist claims that the system is rigged resonate because there is truth in them. Elites are insulated from the worst effects of the cultural and economic dissolution they support. Reno observes that
column2: “For all their talk of an open economy and open society
column3: those in the upper echelons of our society work very hard to protect their children.” Everyone wants a secure future for their children
column4: even if it requires ideological hypocrisy—just look at well-off white liberal parents in New York City and the schools they send their children to.

column1: A broader sense of solidarity no longer informs our culture and economy. We are becoming homeless; a place to live is not the same as a place to belong
column2: and the postwar consensus has deconstructed the sources of belonging. We were told that diversity and inclusion would provide “a home without walls” in which everyone felt welcomed and accepted
column3: but this has not come to pass. Those subjected to these therapies of the open society still seek loyalty and solidarity
column4: which often leads to nurturing grievances and embracing identity politics.

column1: The postwar consensus is in crisis because it is unbalanced; the more dominant it becomes
column2: the more destabilizing its neglect of basic human needs for belonging and solidarity becomes. Reno therefore declares that “We don’t need more diversity and innovation. We need a home. And for that
column3: we will require the return of the strong gods.” The peace and prosperity the postwar consensus promised (and to some degree delivered) is not enough
column4: for humans are not livestock.

column1: Ezra Klein’s Monday article in Vox addressed race in politics
column2: comparing the election of Barack Obama with the election of Donald Trump. It was longer and more nuanced than most of what is published there
column3: but still missed the major point.

column1: The changes in the way race plays into national politics are not a reaction to Obama. They are a reaction to the world progressives built and are still building
column2: a world that has seen the Left’s default position go from aspiring toward color-blindness to one of grievance-nursing along every possible intersectional axis. The political world that gave us Trump is different than the one that gave us Obama
column3: but the difference is of the Left’s own making.

column1: Demographics Aren’t Destiny
Klein begins with the latest version of the demographics-as-destiny argument. That theory was popularized in John Judis and Ruy Teixeira’s 2002 book
column2: “The Emerging Democratic Majority
column3: ” and used to run something like this: as immigration from places other than Europe shifts America’s demographics
column4: the percentage of non-white voters will rise. These voters will vote Democratic with the same uniformity as black Americans currently do
column5: and their votes will eventually be so numerous that they will reduce the Republican Party to a permanent second place.

column1: The next election after Judis and Teixeira’s book debuted was George W. Bush’s electoral and popular vote majority
column2: but theories in the political world are not derailed by mere events. Demographics-as-destiny adherents focused on the “emerging” part of the title and held out hope for the day their favored politicians would win simply by existing and America would become a California writ large. Obama’s 2008 election and somewhat reduced majority in 2012 maintained the fiction
column3: and things looked bright for the Left.

column1: Trump’s election in 2016 changed that
column2: as it changed nearly every working theory of American politics. Writers like Klein did not waver in their belief that Republicans would soon be swamped by numbers of unflinching Democratic voters
column3: but added a corollary: before the apotheosis of progressivism
column4: there would be rear-guard action by the forces of reaction. The ever-racist whites would hold off the forces of goodness and decency until even greater numbers finally swamped them. That
column5: in brief
column6: is the subject of Klein’s latest article.

column1: From Facts To Faction
But even before Trump’s refutation of the theory
column2: there was a shift in the demographics argument’s delivery. The original idea involved political scientists looking at numbers
column3: extrapolating them into the future
column4: and saying what they thought it would mean for the country.

column1: It is not wrong to say these things; facts are facts
column2: trends can be predicted based on them. But the underlying premise should make Americans a little uneasy. People vote as individuals
column3: but progressives too often see them only as groups
column4: the sum of their intersections. The demographic argument suggests that DNA determines our votes more than free will does
column5: in a weird secular pre-destinationism.

column1: The tenor of that argument changed as 2016’s election approached. Neutral recitation of the facts gave way in some writers’ work to gleeful anticipation of white people’s diminution. As the intersectional movement moved from academia to mainstream
column2: some on the far-left dropped the powerful liberal idea of color-blind equality in favor of a system of permanent conflict between races
column3: religions
column4: ethnicities
column5: and classes. All differences were deemed vectors of oppression
column6: and the cause of it all was white people.

column1: Articles of this sort abounded
column2: as in like a 2015 work from Salon (“White guys are killing us”) or a 2016 article from the Huffington Post (“Democrats Don’t Need White Men to Win”). One might argue that these outlets are not the arbiters of mainstream opinion
column3: but one of the leveling effects of the Internet is that any article can go viral.

column1: Establishment lefties might have kept the triumphal attitude out of their pieces
column2: but that discretion did not extend to all corners of their coalition. Since the election
column3: things have only gotten crazier. When these articles and others like them spread through social media
column4: that spirit of ugly
column5: factional
column6: demographic-inspired triumph signaled to left-leaning voters that this sort of open distaste for a large segment of the population was acceptable.

column1: It’s Not Just Demographic Displacement
More importantly
column2: electorally speaking
column3: is that many white Democrats got that message
column4: too. Their party and the Clinton campaign (which were essentially the same thing in 2016) spent all their energy hailing what Ronald Brownstein in 2012 called the “coalition of the ascendant.” But the message filtered down to the people not as one of a rising tide lifting all demographic boats into a new
column5: more equal America
column6: but of one group clambering over another for control of the levers of power.

column1: How many people in the reciprocal “coalition of the descending” could be expected to remain behind in a Democratic Party that gleefully prophesied their fade into insignificance? Having been told that the melting pot was a lie and that their very existence caused oppression along countless intersecting vectors
column2: how many could be expected not to defend themselves?

column1: Among rich lefties
column2: perhaps
column3: this new reality was acceptable
column4: as it dovetailed with their guilt over their own success. But for the middle and working classes
column5: it constituted only a threat
column6: and a demand that they be held responsible for the deeds of an establishment that had never included them or their blue-collar ancestors.

column1: My colleague David Marcus picked up on this point earlier than most
column2: writing in May 2016 that “this shift in rhetoric undermines what was once the core of anti-racist efforts. Treating people equally has given way to making all of us ambassadors for our race. This is a classic theme in critical race theory
column3: that people of color carry a burden of representation that white people do not. But foisting the baggage of representation onto white people doesn’t solve that problem. It makes it worse.”

column1: In abandoning color-blind equality as a goal
column2: the far-left all but dared white people to adopt their theories and emphasize their own racial identity
column3: even over the more unifying identity of our shared Americanism and above even our shared humanity. Sadly
column4: this appealed to some of what became known as the alt-right. The right-wing establishment had adopted the racial equality platform that began on the Left
column5: but instead of consolidating that victory and working together toward greater racial harmony
column6: the Left got more radical

column1: Equality was seen as unachievable
column2: so grievance-balancing intersectionality would take its place. As a bonus
column3: such a system of finely balanced intersectional offenses required constant debate and
column4: ultimately
column5: gatekeepers to determine which historical wrongs were greatest. That gives a small elite a great deal of power
column6: in contrast to the simpler virtue of just leaving people alone and treating everyone equally.

column1: Abandoning equality when they thought it was of no more use to them
column2: they showed their true face to people.

column3: our first black president. While we should not say that one black chief executive signaled the end of racism in America
column4: it does at least signal that a majority of people were not so enthralled by white grievances that they could not elect a black man to be the leader of the free world.

column1: Yet that same electorate’s turn to Trump is seen as evidence that white Americans are relentlessly racist. What could have caused the change? Klein points to the demography
column2: but that has been changing forever and should have helped his side
column3: not hurt it.

column1: The new factor in the electorate equation was the attitude around that demography
column2: and the Left’s premature celebration when they thought the game was won. Abandoning equality when they thought it was of no more use to them
column3: they showed their true face to people
column4: including those to whom equality still meant something.

column1: That
column2: at best
column3: leaves one party still dedicated to that ideal. At worst
column4: it leaves none

column1: The Equation Does Not Balance

column2: Klein and those like him misunderstand the nature of race in politics. Specifically
column3: they think that not only will demographic changes continue into the future
column4: but that 2018’s definitions of race will continue as well.

column1: But history shows that this has never been the case. For a country that has long been preoccupied with race
column2: America’s standard definitions of race have undergone considerable change. They will continue to do so.

column1: Even if the Democrats are correct that they will receive the vast majority of minority votes
column2: they are wrong that our current politically motivated definitions of whiteness and non-whiteness will remain the same. Klein briefly engages with this point
column3: though he ultimately ignores it: “Demographers can and do disagree over whether these projections will hold. Perhaps Hispanic whites will begin identifying simply as whites in the coming years
column4: much as the Irish became white in the 20th century. Race is what we make of it
column5: and what we make of it shifts and mutates.”

column1: For a country that has long been preoccupied with race
column2: America’s standard definitions of race have undergone considerable change.

column1: There’s no “perhaps” about it. This change has been going on forever
column2: and attempts to ignore it are willful blindness motivated by politics. In the twenty-first century
column3: politicos speak of the historical dominance of white people and their oppression of non-whites
column4: but that is not how people thought of themselves in those days.

column1: In Theodore Roosevelt’s time
column2: people in the establishment (including TR himself) spoke not of the white race but of the Anglo-Saxon people. That narrow definition of the people they desired to see in charge of things was big enough to admit other Protestants of colonial heritage (including Roosevelt’s New York Dutch ancestors)
column3: but not enough to admit the Irish
column4: Italians
column5: Jews
column6: Greeks
column7: and Slavs who had made up most of the immigrants over the previous half-century. These
column8: they believed
column9: were utterly foreign and had cultures at odds with American values.

column1: How things changed. Klein notes that the Irish “became white in the 20th century
column2: ” and he is correct. Indeed
column3: the Irish are so thoroughly white that it seems now ridiculous to suggest that they are anything but white. Other groups that immigrated around the same time have likewise been welcomed into the establishment
column4: accessing its societal benefits and costs alike.

column1: There is no reason to believe that other white-looking people like Arabs and Persians will be long excluded. Indeed
column2: their identification as non-white people is primarily a political matter at a time when access to intersectional vectors of oppression is more politically advantageous than “becoming white.” Even the term “white” may be eclipsed by some new artifact of racial ideology or pseudoscience

column1: This goes to show how race is far more a matter of politics and social theory than of biology. No matter what 23andMe says about our DNA
column2: how we view ourselves—and how others view us—is far more mutable. The groups we now call “white” and “people of color” are constructed by political alliances of convenience
column3: not biological facts
column4: just as the so-called Anglo-Saxon people was. Increased intermarriage between whites and non-whites will blur these artificial lines even further. They have changed
column5: and will continue to change.

column1: Racial Grievance Politics Are Already Changing
Already the ground is shifting. Affirmative action
column2: once intended to redress the harms of white discrimination against non-whites
column3: is now being used to limit Asians’ college admission as well. Does that mean they are beginning to be no longer a part of the awkwardly named “people of color” coalition? column1: They encourage people to align their politics to their race instead of their values.
Race is not something that is projectable as a trend
column2: and even discussing it in such fine detail—who is white? who isn’t?—feels kind of gross and un-American. That is the biggest problem with observations like Klein’s: by drawing attention to the many variations within the American people
column3: they exacerbate the divisions between us. By imputing political judgments to entire races
column4: they encourage people to align their politics to their race instead of their values.

column1: The real solution to racial grievances in politics is to return to the old liberal American idea of aspiring toward equality
column2: no matter how difficult that goal may be to attain. Instead of focusing on where people are coming from
column3: let’s talk about where they are headed
column4: who they are in joining the American melting pot and becoming every bit as American as those who were born here.

column2: and Democrats have endorsed that platform for years. They all should reconsider their choices
column3: make politics about ideas
column4: not skin color
column5: and return to the universal American values that once brought us together.";['lefties']

column1: That’s why a new proposal from a bevy of progressive lawmakers comes as a welcome and innovative addition to the policy arsenal: increasing the corporate tax rate in accordance with the gap between CEO pay and median worker pay. Here’s the general idea:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.)
column2: Rep. Barbara Lee (D-Calif.) and Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) introduced the Tax Excessive CEO Pay Act
column3: which rewrites the federal tax code to tackle the inequality crisis created by corporate America’s unrestrained greed. The typical restaurant employee at McDonald’s would have to work for more than 2
column4: 000 years to earn what the company’s CEO Chris Kempczinski received last year. A retail worker at Gap Inc. would have to work for more than 3
column5: 000 years to receive the annual compensation of Gap’s former CEO Art Peck. Peck’s pay was increased by 33 percent in 2018
column6: even after he presided over years of declines in sales and stock prices. The Tax Excessive CEO Pay Act would pressure corporations to curb these outrageous pay gaps that are the norm today
column7: by imposing graduated taxes for companies that pay their CEO more than 50 times the pay of the median worker. The tax penalties would begin at 0.5 percentage points and rise to 5 percentage points for firms compensating their chief executives at more than 500 times the rate of their workers. column8: nutrition assistance
column9: and Medicaid

column1: Becoming Homeless

column2: not to its absence. The immediate danger is not that of dark

column5: but of one that is too open. We are not suffering from too much solidarity and loyalty

column2: “For all their talk of an open economy and open society

column4: for humans are not livestock.

column1: The Anti-Human Consensus
